The micrograph is https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Trypanosoma_sp._PHIL_613_lores.jpg , public-domain because it's a work of an agency of the United States Government.

The building is the Ocean Road Hospital in Dar-es-Salaam, photographed by I.M. Santos (also known as E. M. Santos), about whom further details are pending. It's probably public domain due to its age, but I'm not 100% sure.

item.content:encoded:
I may have missed something but why station someone (Mark Fulu) to this SCP when they cannot properly speak the English language?

Even if there was a drastic personal shortage wouldn't it make sense for this person to be trained in the language before they are even accepted into the foundation?

It seems inconsistent that a single language wouldn't be properly used foundation-wide, not to mention that it could cause issues with coordination and safety issues, for example the organisation of foundation resources and reporting of containment breaches without the use of editing or translation, which would needlessly slow any response.

item.content:encoded:
Grammar is much improved, but there are still several spots of awkward phrasing or insufficiently-clinical tone. Also, the parasite is referred to as a "virus" at one point, and assets in "North America" are referenced, when the article seems to suggest that the SCP is located in Africa, so there are some internal consistency issues. That last series of notes is a clever idea (having heavily-edited notes in English by someone with limited English skills adds a nice touch of authenticity), but: It's clearly trying to imply something happening with the Zone of Denial, but there's no payoff.

Now that the grammar is good enough for me to read through the whole thing, I definitely like the concept, but this still needs some serious editing.

You repeat "zone of denial" so many times it becomes a headache to read. A smoother phrase or some synonyms would go a long way.

The addendum about why you haven't demolished the hospital seems, to me, a bit extraneous. It is understood that we don't just randomly destroy SCPs; there really isn't any need to discuss it unless it is given keter status, since keters are usually the only ones the Foundation even considers actively trying to destroy.

item.content:encoded:
Well, maybe "sloppy" isn't the best term for it, but there's no structure to the end there.

First we've got Addendum SCP-793:XOJ1 where some researchers are trying to say this is actually safe (that is where the smiley is) and then we've got a bunch of urgent missives for help about a moving zone from someone who speaks limited English.

It's disjointed, contradictory, and does not add to the feeling of the piece.

There's just a lot of extra wording that could be pruned down and concepts that can be communicated without extra documentation. For example, there can be a tiny line about how someone on site is claiming the zone shifts to replace all that stuff at the end.

item.content:encoded:
If you need to refer to the Foundation in a document call it the Foundation rather than the SCP. The SCP is what we do, the Foundation is what we are.

Damn good point. Author, go fix that immediately.

I dunno that I agree about sloppiness. And I'm not finding a smiley…

Woop, found it. and a lot of other things. Here, I'll point out the worst of it.

The stakes are to have signs emplaced on them to not enter this area without Class D SCP authorization

Author, go read this page. Class D authorization is not a thing.

Controversy over the expungement of Euclid-class SCP specimens has always been a topic of discussion with SCP personnel ever since the SCP's foundation, SCP-793 being one such example. The general consensus about Euclid-class expungement appears to regard SCP-793 as "Not to be demolished", and we agree, albeit there has been still some controversy over the topic.

I'm honestly not sure what you're trying to say here. "expungement" around here is a word meaning "censorship of documents". I think you might be looking for a word meaning "destruction", and even then it's a weird distracted ramble you might as well just cut since it doesn't have anything to do with the SCP object in question.

B) The hospital's architectural structure appears to be continually sturdy and shows no signs of serious decay, suggesting structural invulnerability. We don't think this should be tested, though! ;)

Please remember that you're writing a reference document for a group of professionals. Jokey tone doesn't fit, and I'm pretty certain someone in character just got fired for that winky face.

Fix those and you'll be pretty okay, though.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
So.

First off, let me say I really, really, really like the concept of a ghost disease. As far as I know that's never been done before, so good work. I was ready to upvote this, until I came to this section right here:

A final notation about possible human death as the result of SCP-793's actions - the "reversal effects" do reverse victim death, in totality. Once a dead victim is rescued from the maximum reproductive zone, somatic cells appear immediatly and remaining parisites are removed from existence. Upon so-called "undeath", individuals recall extreme pain in their bodily reconstruction (mostly regarded as something along the lines "thousands of knives peircing his/her body") and no recollection of ever entering the zone of denial or any knowledge of SCP-793.

That ruined it. By removing the risk of real death, to me you remove the horror from the concept. I realize that may be an individual opinion, but I do ask that you consider revising or simply expunging that section. While the idea of a hospital surrounded by corpses up to a certain point does have a certain macabre charm, I just… enh. Sleeping sickness' victims are usually ambulatory for at least enough time to get out of the ZoD.

Secondly, the name "zone of denial". It's possible I missed something important, but why is it called that?
